newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Vranitzky vows CA decision soon after Jan 10.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Vranitzky vows CA decision soon after Jan 10.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky on Wednesday threw his weight behind a pledge that a decision on selling the Creditanstalt bank group must come soon after a January 10 deadline.

"A decision must be made swiftly after the 10th for the best bidder and the highest offer. We're committed to that," Vranitzky told a news conference opening the Social Democratic Party's annual convention in this southern Austrian spa town.
He declined to be drawn on a specific date for the sale decision but added: "If we let it drag on, it would hardly conjure up a good impression of the decision-making capacity of the government."
The privatisation of Creditanstalt, the country's second biggest bank, was first planned in 1991.
Finance Minister Viktor Klima, in charge of the sale, has given three existing bidders for the state's 70 percent stake in Creditanstalt until Friday to improve their bids.
The Social Democrat's junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party, has called for a special session of parliament on January 14 to discuss the contentious sale.
The conservatives want the bank, long regarded as a preserve of the right, to be sold to an international group of bidders led by insurer EA-Generali.
But the dominant Social Democrats strongly prefer a sale to market leader Bank Austria, which has topped EA-Generali's bid by almost three billion schillings.
"We can't pass up on one billion schillings -- let alone three to four billion. We need it, otherwise we'd have to get it from elsewhere," Vranitzky said.

The conservatives say a sale to Bank Austria would not be a genuine privatisation because the bank is effectively controlled by the Social Democrat-ruled City of Vienna through its Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ) foundation.

AVZ directly owns around 46 percent of Bank Austria voting shares, or 40 percent of total equity, and indirectly influences a clear majority. It also guarantees the bank's liabilities, ensuring it an AAA credit rating.
"(Vienna mayor Michael) Haeupl told me today that he is prepared, and wants, to reduce AVZ's stake in Bank Austria to below 25 percent," Vranitzky said.
Conservative leader Wolfgang Schuessel said he could only foresee a sale to Bank Austria if the City of Vienna withdrew fully from Bank Austria.

The chancellor said it was solely up to the finance minister to choose the winner. "I stress again it is Klima's decision and it is independent from the special parliamentary session. We are not going to be bullied into a decision."
The finance minister's hands are also bound by European Union law, which dictates that the highest price wins.

The chancellor flatly rejected a compromise solution offered by the People's Party on Tuesday, according to which half the state's stake in Creditanstalt would be sold to Bank Austria and the rest floated on the stock exchange.
"This is a bad option...the law dictates that we sell to the highest bidder," Vranitzky said.
